blocks.text: Response formatting steps back from any single format, JSON, XML, or markdown, all covered in earlier topics, to the broader decision of which format actually fits a given response, based on who or what is actually going to consume it, and how to keep that choice consistent across an application.

This topic covers identifying the real consumer of a response, choosing among the available formats, handling hybrid responses that combine formats, keeping formatting consistent across a conversation, and practical concerns like streaming and truncation.
1. Response Formatting as a Higher Level Decision

blocks.alt: Building on schema-based outputs, response formatting is about choosing the right format overall

blocks.text: While earlier topics in this module covered the mechanics of JSON, XML, and markdown individually, response formatting is the practical decision layer above them, which of these formats, or a combination, actually fits a specific response.
2. Identifying the Actual Consumer

blocks.alt: A human reads it directly, an application parses it programmatically, or both consume the same response

blocks.text: The first question worth asking is who or what actually consumes this response, a person reading it directly in a chat interface, application code parsing it programmatically, or sometimes both, a response displayed to a user that also needs to be logged and analyzed by a system.
3. Choosing Among the Available Formats

blocks.alt: JSON, XML, markdown, and plain text are the main format choices

blocks.text: JSON and XML, both covered in earlier topics, suit machine consumption, markdown suits human readable display, and plain unformatted text remains a reasonable choice for very short, simple responses where any structure would be unnecessary overhead.

blocks.text: 4. Hybrid Responses, Markdown Wrapping JSON

blocks.alt: A markdown explanation wraps an embedded JSON code block inside it

blocks.text: A common practical pattern for a response both a human and a program need serves both audiences at once, a markdown explanation for the human reader, with a JSON code block embedded inside it containing the exact structured data an application can reliably extract and parse.

code.content:
## Analysis Summary

The document appears to be a valid contract with no major issues.

```json
{"valid": true, "issues_found": 0}
```

blocks.text: 5. Formatting Consistency Across a Conversation

blocks.alt: Turn 1 uses one format, turn 2 uses a different, inconsistent format

blocks.text: A response format that shifts unpredictably from one turn to the next, plain text in one response, markdown in the next, for what is functionally the same kind of request, creates a confusing, unpredictable experience, this connects to the system prompt design covered in an earlier topic, stating the expected format once in the system prompt keeps it consistent across every turn.
6. Streaming Considerations

blocks.alt: A streaming response has partial content arriving incrementally

blocks.text: For an application streaming a response token by token as it generates, a format that only becomes valid once fully complete, like a JSON object, is harder to usefully display incrementally than markdown or plain text, which can be shown progressively as it streams in, this is a real practical consideration when choosing a format for a live, streaming user experience.

blocks.title: This is a genuine tradeoff worth planning for upfront
blocks.content: A strict machine parseable format like JSON generally needs to be received in full before it can be reliably parsed, while markdown or plain text can be displayed to a user incrementally as it streams, the right choice depends on whether the response needs to stream live or can be delivered all at once.

blocks.text: 7. Truncation Risk and Response Format

blocks.alt: A response truncated mid structure creates a broken parsing risk

blocks.text: If a response gets cut off before completing, due to hitting a maximum output length or a network interruption, a structured format like JSON or XML becomes unparseable entirely, since it was never fully closed, plain text or markdown degrades more gracefully, remaining at least partially readable even if incomplete.
8. Connecting Back to Output Format

This topic builds directly on the Output Format component covered in an earlier module, response formatting is really that same idea applied with a broader, more deliberate decision process, considering the actual consumer, consistency, and practical delivery concerns rather than picking a format by default.
9. A Practical Decision Framework

A reasonable starting framework, ask who consumes the response, if only an application, use JSON or XML with a schema where possible, if only a person, use markdown or plain text, if both, consider a hybrid response, and in every case, check whether streaming or truncation risk should influence the final choice.
Worked Example

A team building a customer support tool originally returns plain JSON for every response, including ones displayed directly to support agents, agents find the raw JSON hard to scan quickly during a live call.

Switching to a hybrid response, a markdown summary for the agent to read directly, with the underlying structured data embedded as a JSON code block for the application to log and analyze, serves both the agent readability need and the application parsing need from a single response.
Common Mistakes

items: Defaulting to the same format for every response without considering who or what actually consumes it
Letting response format shift inconsistently across turns for functionally similar requests
Choosing a strict format like JSON for a response that needs to stream progressively to a user in real time
Not considering truncation risk when choosing between a structured format and a more gracefully degrading one

blocks.text: Practice

Take a response your application currently generates, identify who or what actually consumes it, a person, a program, or both, and decide whether the current format is genuinely the best fit or whether a hybrid response would serve the actual audience better.
Key Takeaway

Response formatting is the practical decision of choosing among JSON, XML, markdown, plain text, or a hybrid combination based on who actually consumes a response, kept consistent across a conversation, and chosen with real practical concerns like streaming and truncation risk in mind, rather than defaulting to one format for every situation.
